passages.title: The Scorer’s Box
paras: The summer I turned twelve, I became the scorer for my brother’s under 14 cricket team.
The scorer’s box at Kooringal Oval was a tin shed with a sliding window and two stools.
I would share it with Mrs Vu, who had scored for the club for nineteen years.
I had watched a lot of cricket on television, so I was sure the job would be easy.
Mrs Vu handed me a pencil, not a pen.
“Every ball goes in the book,” she said.
“Watch the umpire’s arms.
They tell you what to write.”
A ball that rolled over the rope was worth four, she explained, and one that cleared it in the air was worth six.
Most overs would be quiet, but a few would bring three things at once.
For the first hour, I kept up easily.
Then a bowler began sending down wides, and the batters started running twos.
I wrote faster and faster, and twice I looked at the wrong line.
Mrs Vu said nothing.
Now and then she tapped her own book with her pencil, which I took to mean that she wanted me to hurry up.
At the drinks break, the umpire came to the window and asked for the score.
I read out 87.
Mrs Vu read out 85, and my face went hot.
She turned her book towards me and ran her finger down the last over, ball by ball, until she stopped at a four.
In my book, it was a six.
“That one fooled me too, my first year,” Mrs Vu said.
I knew she was only being kind.
Nobody who had scored for nineteen years could ever have mixed up a four and a six.
I rubbed out my six and wrote a four, and the umpire wrote 85 on his card.
In the second half, I watched Mrs Vu more than the game.
Whenever the umpire raised an arm, she tapped her book once before she wrote anything.
It was not a signal to hurry.
It was a signal to look up.
After that, I looked up every time she tapped, and our totals matched at every break.
At the end of the season, I helped clear out the club cupboard and found a pile of old scorebooks.
The oldest had Mrs Vu’s name on the cover.
On its third page, a six had been rubbed out and a four written over the top.
I never asked her about it.
I just put the book back where I had found it.

passages.title: The Bin Chicken Comes to Town
paras: Walk through a city park in Sydney or Brisbane at lunchtime and you may meet a tall white bird with a bald black head and a long curved bill.
Quite often, that bill is buried deep in a rubbish bin.
This is the Australian white ibis, which many people call the "bin chicken", and not always kindly.
Some people find them funny and others find them a nuisance, but very few know where they came from.
Fifty years ago, hardly anyone in these cities had ever seen one.
For thousands of years, the white ibis lived mostly on the wetlands of inland Australia, such as the swamps and floodplains along the Murray and Darling rivers.
There it waded through shallow water, probing the mud with its bill for yabbies, insects and frogs.
When floods filled the swamps, huge flocks gathered to nest among the reeds, sometimes tens of thousands of birds in one place.
Over the last century, much of that water was taken away.
Dams and channels sent river water to farms and towns, so the swamps flooded less often.
Then long droughts dried out many of the wetlands that were left.
With fewer places to nest and less food in the mud, many ibis left the inland and flew toward the coast.
What they found there suited them well.
City parks have lawns to probe and ponds to wade in, a little like a smaller, tidier swamp.
Rubbish tips, picnic tables and open bins offer scraps every day of the year, whether it has rained or not.
So many of the birds that arrived did not move on.
They stayed, built nests in the tall palm trees of city parks and raised their young there.
The ibis's bill helps explain its success.
It is long, thin and curved, made for reaching into mud and narrow cracks.
The same shape slides easily under a bin lid or into the corner of a chip packet.
Some birds have even learnt that a picnic blanket means food, and they will stroll right up to a family to wait for a crust.
Not everyone is pleased to have them as neighbours.
Ibis can be noisy, their nests smell, and a large flock can leave a picnic area covered in droppings.
Some councils have trimmed the palm trees where the birds nest.
Others have put in new bins with heavy lids that a beak cannot lift, and many parks now ask visitors not to share their lunch, because a bird that is fed once will keep coming back.
Meanwhile, scientists who count waterbirds on the inland wetlands have found far fewer ibis nesting there than in the past.
That worries some of them.
The crowds of ibis in our parks can look like a success story.
They may instead be a sign that the birds have lost the homes they really need.

passages.title: Switch Off the School Bell
paras: At my school, the bell rings 11 times a day.
It rings when classes start and when they finish, when recess begins and when it ends, and twice more at lunch.
It is loud and harsh, and it never cares what is happening in the room.
Last week it cut my science teacher off halfway through the most interesting sentence of the term.
Some days it feels as if our whole school runs to the bell, not to the clock.
I think our school should switch the bell off for good.
Plenty of schools around Australia already have, and nothing terrible has happened.
Their students still get to class on time, and their days still run to the minute.
The first reason is that a school without bells would be calmer.
When a bell rings, hundreds of students stand up at the same second and pour into the same corridors.
Bags swing, doors bang and everyone talks over everyone else.
Without a bell, classes do not all finish at the same second.
They leave a minute or two apart, so the corridors never fill all at once, and the rush simply disappears.
The second reason is that lessons would no longer be cut short.
A bell does not know that a class is one minute away from finishing an experiment or reading the last page of a chapter.
A teacher does.
Without a bell, teachers could end each lesson at a sensible point instead of stopping mid sentence.
Third, students would learn to manage their own time.
After school, no bell tells you when to leave for training or when your bus goes.
Without a bell, students have to check a clock and think ahead, and that is a skill they will use for the rest of their lives.
Not everyone agrees.
Some people worry that students will wander into class late.
Others say that teachers will run over time and eat into recess.
A few parents have asked how new Year 7 students in a big school would know when to move.
Ms Okafor is the principal of a school in Geelong that switched off its bells three years ago.
She told me that these worries faded within a term.
Lateness dropped, because students stopped waiting for a bell to tell them to move and started watching the clock for themselves.
Every classroom now has a large clock above the door, and the teachers agreed to finish on time so that recess is never cut short.
A school bell made sense a hundred years ago, when few students owned a watch.
Today there is a clock on every classroom wall.
It is time our school trusted its students to read one.
Switch off the bell, and let the day run a little more quietly.

passages.title: A Year at the Seed Library
paras: Next to the returns chute at Bellwood Library stands an old wooden cabinet with 60 small drawers.
It once held cards for finding books.
Now the drawers hold paper packets of seeds.
Anyone with a library card can borrow up to five packets at a time, grow the plants at home, and bring back seeds from their best plants at the end of the season.
The scheme began two years ago, and this report looks at how its second year went.
Members borrowed 1,240 packets over the year.
Tomatoes were the favourite by a long way, making up almost a third of all loans, with beans and pumpkins well behind.
Herbs such as basil and coriander were borrowed less often, but the people who took them usually came back for more.
In a short survey, many borrowers said they had never grown anything from seed before.
Several said they only signed up after a neighbour showed them a crop of beans over the fence.
Bringing seeds back is the hard part.
Of the 1,240 packets, seeds came back from 410, about one in three.
Beans and pumpkins were the easiest to save, because their seeds are large and dry.
Most of the pumpkin packets came back with seeds, often in jars with the grower's name on the lid.
Tomato seeds were much harder.
They sit inside wet pulp, so they have to be soaked, rinsed and dried before they can be stored, and many borrowers found this too fiddly.
Every batch that comes back is tested before it goes into a drawer.
A volunteer counts out ten seeds, rolls them in a damp paper towel and leaves them in a warm cupboard for a week.
If fewer than seven sprout, the batch fails.
Seeds that fail the test are not thrown out: they go to the primary school next door, where students plant them in cups to see what comes up.
Winter was the quiet season.
Few people plant in the cold months, and 12 of the 60 drawers sat empty from June to August.
Librarian Grace Mbeki used the time to sort the cabinet by season instead of by alphabet, so that a borrower in spring could see straight away what was ready to plant.
Not everything went to plan.
A batch labelled as climbing beans turned out to be bush beans, and some borrowers built tall frames for plants that never grew past their knees.
Since then, volunteers have glued a photo of the grown plant onto every packet, and everyone who built a frame was given a free packet of real climbing beans.
Next year the library hopes to add native plants, such as saltbush and everlasting daisies, which suit Bellwood's dry summers.
It also plans a seed saving morning in late summer, where members who have managed to save tomato seeds will show everyone else how it is done.

passages.title: Three Every Morning
paras: The lemon tree in Tomasi's backyard dropped more fruit than his family could ever use.
By June the grass under it was dotted with yellow, and Mum had started leaving bags of lemons at the school gate.
“If one more person gives me a lemon cake recipe,” she said, “I'll scream.”
Three weeks earlier, on the last day of the holidays, Tomasi and his little brother Elias had been playing cricket in the yard.
Tomasi hit the best shot of his life.
The ball sailed over the side fence into Mrs Petrakis's garden, and a moment later they heard a sharp crack.
Elias looked at Tomasi.
Tomasi looked at the fence.
Then they both went inside and turned the television up very loud.
Mrs Petrakis lived next door with a grey cat and a vegetable patch she weeded every afternoon.
The next morning, one pane of her kitchen window was covered with a square of cardboard, held in place with brown tape.
It stayed there for days.
Tomasi walked past it on his way to the bus and kept his eyes on the footpath.
That was when the lemons started.
Every morning before school, Tomasi slipped out the front while it was still half dark, picked the three best lemons he could find, and set them in a neat row on Mrs Petrakis's front step.
He never knocked.
Once he heard her slippers in the hallway and ran so fast that he left a school shoe on her path, and had to creep back for it ten minutes later.
Elias found out on the fourth day.
“Why are you giving her lemons?” he whispered.
“We've got heaps,” said Tomasi.
“Mum keeps saying so.”
Elias thought about this for a while.
“That's not why,” he said.
On Saturday, Mum sent Tomasi next door with a bag of lemons, and Mrs Petrakis opened the door before he could knock.
Behind her, on the kitchen bench, sat a glass bowl piled high with lemons, every one of them shiny and yellow.
“Someone has been leaving me presents,” she said.
“Three every morning, lined up like soldiers.”
She looked at the bag in his hands, and then at his face.
Tomasi felt his ears go hot.
Then she picked something up from the windowsill and held it out.
It was a red cricket ball, scuffed on one side.
“This landed in my garden,” she said.
“I think it belongs to whoever has been leaving the lemons.
Tell them the glass man comes on Tuesday, and that I've been paid back already.”
Tomasi took the ball.
He opened his mouth, closed it again, and nodded.
On the way home he walked straight past the lemon tree without picking a single one.
That night he set his alarm for the usual time, then turned it off again.

passages.title: The Window by the Path
paras: In Year 5 I started learning the trumpet, and our band teacher, Ms Tran, said that if I wanted to catch up with the others I would have to practise every lunchtime.
So every day, when the bell went, I ate my sandwich in four bites, unlocked the music room and played until the end of lunch, alone, with the window open because the room was always hot.
Outside that window was the path to the caretaker’s shed, and the caretaker was Mr Nikolaidis.
He was older than my grandparents and wore a flat grey cap, even on the hottest days.
I had said hello to him once, near the bins, and he had nodded without smiling.
That was all the proof I needed that he did not like me.
Every lunchtime, while I practised, I could see the top of that grey cap moving slowly past the bottom of the window.
He was always out there while I played, sweeping the same short stretch of path.
Once, when I stopped to rest my lips, I heard him whistling the tune I had just been playing.
Then the shed door banged shut.
I decided that Mr Nikolaidis was keeping watch so that he could complain to the principal about the noise.
I started closing the window, even on hot days, and playing more quietly, which Ms Tran said was the opposite of what a trumpet was for.
Near the end of term, I came in one lunchtime and found a small pencil circle on my music, around a note in the fourth line, the high note I always missed.
I decided Ms Tran must have drawn it during band and I had not noticed.
I kept practising, a little more carefully than before.
On the last day of term, Ms Tran stopped me at the music room door with a strange look on her face.
“Mr Nikolaidis came to see me,” she said.
“He asked whether you’d like someone to practise with.
His granddaughter Eleni is coming to live with him, and she plays the clarinet.
She starts here next term.”
I didn’t know what to say, so I said, “Okay.”
Eleni and I practised together every lunchtime for the rest of the year, with the window wide open, and Mr Nikolaidis never complained once.
Some days he brought an old chair out of the shed and sat on it to listen.
It was years later, when Eleni and I were both grown up, that she told me the rest.
Her grandfather had drawn that pencil circle himself, she said.
He had played the trumpet in a town band in Greece when he was young, and he had swept that path every lunchtime because he missed the sound.
“He told me you had a lovely tone,” Eleni said, “and terrible timing.”
I thought about the grey cap moving past the window, and how sure I had been about what it meant.

passages.title: Steering Without a Wheel
paras: Every March, the sky over Canberra fills with hot air balloons.
For about a week, dozens of them lift off from the lawns near Lake Burley Griffin just after dawn, some shaped like teardrops and some like houses, animals or giant faces.
Crowds come early to watch them rise.
Very few of the people watching stop to wonder how a balloon with no engine and no steering wheel ends up where its pilot wants it to go.
The idea behind a hot air balloon is simple.
Hot air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so it rises, and if enough of it is trapped inside a big enough bag, it can lift the bag, a basket and the people in it.
A gas burner above the pilot’s head heats the air inside the balloon.
To go up, the pilot fires the burner.
To come down, the pilot lets the air cool, or opens a flap at the top to let some of it out.
The first hot air balloon to carry passengers rose from the grounds of a French palace in September 1783.
Its passengers were a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
Nobody knew whether living things could survive so high in the air, so the animals went first.
They landed safely about eight minutes later.
Two months after that, in November, two men made the first free flight by people, drifting across Paris for about 25 minutes.
Going up and coming down were solved in 1783.
Going sideways is a different problem, and in a way it has never been solved at all.
A balloon cannot push itself through the air the way a plane can.
It travels inside the wind, at the same speed as the wind, which is why passengers often say the ride feels perfectly still.
There is no breeze in your face, because you are moving with it.
So how do pilots choose where to go?
They use height.
The wind is often blowing in different directions at different heights: near the ground it might be moving north, while a few hundred metres up it might be moving east.
By rising or sinking, a pilot can pick the layer of wind that is heading the right way.
Before a flight, many pilots let go of a small helium balloon and watch which way it drifts as it climbs.
This tells them what each layer of air is doing.
That is also why balloons fly so early.
Just after sunrise, the air near the ground is usually cool and calm.
As the sun warms the ground during the morning, warm air begins to rise in bumpy columns, and the winds grow stronger and harder to predict.
A pilot who takes off at dawn has a few smooth hours before that happens.
Even so, no pilot can promise where a flight will finish.
Most flights end in a paddock or a park, with a chase car that has followed along the roads below.
A good pilot can come down within a few hundred metres of the spot they planned.
A great one, people in the sport like to say, plans to be surprised.

passages.title: Ziggy Explains
paras: Let me be clear. This is my house.
The people are here to open tins
and to warm the couch before I need it.
They are slow, but they are trained.
On Tuesday the big suitcase
came down from the top of the cupboard.
The tall one filled it with towels
and the floppy hats that smell of salt.
I sat in it until they gave up.
On Wednesday the small one knelt down,
held up all her fingers, then folded three away.
“Seven sleeps, Ziggy,” she said.
I do not know what seven is.
I think it may be a kind of fish.
On Thursday they gave the lady next door
a key on a red ribbon
and a list with my name on it, twice.
She smiled at me the way people smile at dogs.
On Friday they left. They took the suitcase
and the hats, and they did not take me,
which proves what I have always suspected:
they have gone to find a better cat.
They will not find one.
The lady next door comes twice a day,
shakes the biscuit tin and talks to me
in a silly voice. I do not come out.
The house is mine now, all of it.
I have chosen to sleep in the tall one’s jumper,
the blue one at the bottom of his bed,
because it is the warmest. That is the only reason.
